title: Your Memories Aren't as Accurate as You Think They Are
author: Marc Smith
summary: Marc Smith opens with a personal, jarring example of false memory, believing he watched the TV show Heroes with his late partner Vanessa, only to discover the show premiered a year after her death, and uses it to introduce the cognitive science of memory reconstruction relevant to classroom learning and retrieval. Drawing on Ulric Neisser's parallel error about a Pearl Harbor memory and on Brainerd and Reyna's fuzzy trace theory, he explains that memories are not stored as fixed copies but consolidated into two simultaneous traces, a detailed verbatim trace that fades quickly and a general gist trace that persists, with false memories arising when the two blend and gaps get filled with plausible but incorrect detail. Smith draws an explicit analogy between this human gap-filling and AI hallucination, noting both systems generate a plausible-seeming but false detail to complete an incomplete pattern. He closes by reframing memory's imprecision as functionally useful rather than purely a flaw: because gist memory strips away episodic specifics, it produces the generalized, transferable knowledge structures that actually support learning, meaning the goal of instruction is not perfectly accurate recall but flexible, adaptable knowledge networks, with implications for how teachers should think about retrieval practice and eyewitness-style questioning of students.
points: Smith's central claim, drawn from Brainerd and Reyna's fuzzy trace theory, is that gist and verbatim memory traces form simultaneously but decay at different rates, verbatim memory fades quickly while gist memory persists, which explains why false memories often feel just as vivid and confident as true ones.

His direct comparison of human memory gap-filling to AI hallucination ('Just like ChatGPT, my brain added this false detail to fill a gap') gives teachers a vivid, transferable analogy for explaining both memory reconstruction and AI unreliability in one framework.

The piece has a specific pedagogical implication: because gist memory is what supports transfer of a concept from one context to another, imperfect, generalized recall is not a failure of learning but is functionally what makes knowledge usable in new situations.

Smith flags a practical risk for classroom questioning and assessment: how a question is phrased can act as a memory 'cue' that nudges a student's recollection toward a false answer, an implication relevant to interrogation-style recall testing.

He notes documented individual-difference risk factors for false-memory susceptibility, including PTSD, lower measured intelligence, older age, and belief in claims that violate established facts, connecting the cognitive-science content to real assessment and wellbeing considerations for specific student populations.
quotes: My fact-checking highlighted two startling errors of memory. Heroes premiered in 2006, a year after Vanessa died, which would have made our son five years old. The knowledge of us watching it together was false.
Memories aren't carbon copies of events; they're reconstructions.
Because of this stripping away of details, many of our recollections appear more as vague resemblances than accurate memories.

LLMs do this as well, which is one reason why they're prone to hallucination. When I recalled watching Heroes, I assumed I was with someone, and the only plausible person was Vanessa. Just like ChatGPT, my brain added this false detail to fill a gap.
According to fuzzy trace theory, both this gist and verbatim memories form simultaneously, but we can store the gist memory after only processing a fraction of their details.
Your questions might act as cues that nudge my memory, but they might also lead me astray... But over time, the verbatim memory will fade more rapidly than the gist memory.

The goal of learning isn't necessarily to create highly accurate memories of learning events, but to form flexible, adaptable and efficient networks of knowledge. The brain has, therefore, evolved to forget almost as much as it has evolved to remember.
